title: Commonwealth Edison Company submits Request for Rehearing of the 09/22/2026 Order under ER26-3257.

documents.name: 2026-10-22 - ER26-2357 - ComEd Rehearing Request.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                   )
Commonwealth Edison Company                        )         Docket No. ER26-3257-001
                                                   )

                            REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF
                          COMMONWEALTH EDISON COMPANY

        Commonwealth Edison Company (“ComEd”) demonstrated in its Notice of Cancellation

(“Notice”) that cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement (“TSA”) with PowerHouse

Hillwood Holding, LLC (“Hillwood”) is just, reasonable, and critical for protecting Illinois

customers for two independent reasons. First, there is no longer a need for the TSA because

ComEd terminated Hillwood’s underlying retail service application (“Retail Application”).

Second, Hillwood refused to post a $594 million letter of credit as required by the TSA to protect

ComEd’s customers. Citing the pendency of a related dispute in federal court in Illinois, the

Commission, however, “decline[d] to exercise primary jurisdiction” and “reject[ed]” the Notice

“without prejudice.”1 That is true even though the federal judge had already deferred to the

Commission’s primary jurisdiction. The Commission’s Order is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary

to law for three primary reasons.

        First, the Commission has no authority under Federal Power Act (“FPA”) Section 205 to

reject the Notice without prejudice on primary jurisdiction grounds. The Commission must

“accept or reject [a] proposal,”2 and it can only reject a filing “if it finds that the changes proposed

by the public utility are not ‘just and reasonable.’”3 To do otherwise ignores Section 205’s


1
  Commonwealth Edison Co., 196 FERC ¶ 61,226, at PP 26, 28-29 (2026) (“Order”).
2
  NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 114 (D.C. Cir. 2017); Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v.
FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 663 (D.C. Cir. 2017).
3
  Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 9 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (citation omitted).
 reticulated procedures and impermissibly tolls Section 205’s 60-day clock for Commission action. 4

The Commission cannot reject a Section 205 submission “without prejudice” to allow for

resolution elsewhere at a later time. Moreover, the Commission’s jurisdiction under Section 205

is exclusive, not concurrent, which precludes the Commission from declining primary jurisdiction.

          Second, the Order failed to consider that the TSA is cancellable based on ComEd’s

termination of Hillwood’s Retail Application, a ground premised on undisputed facts. As ComEd

explained, cancelling the TSA following termination of the Retail Application is just and

reasonable because the TSA expressly confirms that its very existence is derivative of an active

Retail Application. Without an active Retail Application, there is no active request for retail

service, no project being developed, and no need for a TSA. Because the Commission could have

accepted the Notice based on the terminated Retail Application alone, the Commission had no

basis in law or fact to ignore this ground for cancellation, decline to consider it on primary

jurisdiction grounds, or reject the Notice.

          Third, the Commission abused its discretion and failed to engage in reasoned

decisionmaking by summarily declining to exercise primary jurisdiction, reaching the opposite

conclusion from the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. The Commission fell

far short of its obligation to explain its exercise of discretion and departure from precedent.

          For these reasons and those discussed below, the Commission’s Order is arbitrary,

capricious, and contrary to law. The Commission should grant rehearing and accept the Notice

effective July 25, 2026, as requested.




4
    16 U.S.C. § 824d(d).

                                                  2
              STATEMENT OF ISSUES AND SPECIFICATIONS OF ERRORS

       Pursuant to Rule 713(c)(2), 18 C.F.R. § 385.713(c)(2), ComEd provides the following

statement of issues:

       1. The Commission’s Order is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law because it
          declined to exercise primary jurisdiction and rejected the Notice without prejudice
          rather than adjudicating its merits under FPA Section 205. E.g., Atl. City Elec. Co. v.
          FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 9 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (The Commission can reject a Section 205 filing
          “only if it finds that the changes proposed by the public utility are not ‘just and
          reasonable.’” (emphasis added and citation omitted)); NRG Power Mktg., LLC v.
          FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 113 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (The Commission “must accept proposed
          rate changes filed under Section 205 so long as the changes are just and reasonable.”);
          Semtek Int’l Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 531 U.S. 497, 505 (2001) (“[A]n
          ‘adjudication upon the merits’ is the opposite of a ‘dismissal without prejudice[.]’”).

       2. The Commission’s Order is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law because in
          declining to exercise primary jurisdiction and rejecting the Notice without prejudice,
          the Commission has indefinitely suspended ComEd’s proposed rate change, contrary
          to FPA Section 205. 16 U.S.C. § 824d(d) (“Unless the Commission otherwise orders,
          no change shall be made by any public utility in any such rate, charge, classification,
          or service, or in any rule, regulation, or contract relating thereto, except after sixty days’
          notice to the Commission and to the public.”); Allegheny Def. Project v. FERC, 964
          F.3d 1, 15 (D.C. Cir. 2020) (en banc) (By using tolling orders, “[t]he Commission has
          rewritten the statute to say that its failure to act within [a statutorily prescribed time]
          means nothing; it can take as much time as it wants; and until it chooses to act, the
          applicant is trapped[.]”).

       3. The Commission’s Order is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law because the
          Commission has exclusive jurisdiction to determine whether ComEd’s Notice is just
          and reasonable and cannot defer that question to a federal court on primary jurisdiction
          grounds. E.g., Nantahala Power & Light Co. v. Thornburg, 476 U.S. 953, 966 (1986)
          (“FERC clearly has exclusive jurisdiction over the rates to be charged [to] interstate
          wholesale customers.”); In re FirstEnergy Sols. Corp., 945 F.3d 431, 443-44 (6th Cir.
          2019) (FERC’s “plenary and exclusive jurisdiction over wholesale power rates, terms,
          and conditions of service . . . includes all contractual provisions . . . .”); United States
          v. W. Pac. R.R. Co., 352 U.S. 59, 63-64 (1956) (“‘Primary jurisdiction,’ . . . applies
          where a claim is originally cognizable in the courts[.]”).




                                                  3
            4. The Commission’s Order is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law because it
              declined primary jurisdiction and rejected ComEd’s Notice without prejudice without
              considering an independent basis for cancellation—namely, the termination of the
              Retail Application. E.g., Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut.
              Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (Agency rules are “arbitrary and capricious if
              the agency . . . entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem[.]”).

           5.    The Commission’s Order is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law because it did
                not adequately justify its decision to decline to exercise primary jurisdiction over the
                TSA’s interpretation dispute, applying the Arkla factors, Ark. La. Gas Co. v. Hall, 7
                FERC ¶ 61,175, at 61,322-23 (1979), and departed from prior precedent without
                explanation, where: (1) four Commissioners’ concurrences highlight that the policy
                issue underlying the Notice is of paramount importance to the Commission; (2) the
                Commission has deep expertise in the purpose of requiring developers to post security
                in interconnection agreements and industry standards for such requirements; and
                (3) ComEd used similar language in multiple other agreements. E.g., Emera Maine v.
                FERC, 854 F.3d 9, 22 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (Commission orders must reflect “a principled
                and reasoned decision supported by the evidentiary record” (citation omitted)); Am.
                Whitewater v. FERC, 183 F.4th 805, 817 (D.C. Cir. 2026) (“[A]n agency must provide
                a reasoned explanation for departing from precedent or treating similar situations
                differently[.]” (cleaned up)).

                                    REQUEST FOR REHEARING

I.        The Federal Power Act Does Not Permit the Commission to Reject a Section 205
          Filing Without Prejudice on Primary Jurisdiction Grounds.

           The Commission’s decision to “reject the Notice of Cancellation, without prejudice”

 violates its obligations under FPA Section 205. The sole basis for the Commission’s decision to

 decline to assert primary jurisdiction was a purported “dispute over the interpretation of a

 jurisdictional contract,” part of which is being “litigat[ed] in federal district court,” which the

 Commission found sufficient to trigger its discretion under the Arkla factors.5 But this approach

 of simply deciding not to decide whether the Notice is just and reasonable—and to do so for an

 indefinite period—is inconsistent with Section 205 in three respects.



 5
     Order at PP 1, 26-27.

                                                     4
        First, the Order cannot be squared with Section 205’s requirement that the Commission

reject a Section 205 filing only if it finds the filing is unjust and unreasonable. Section 205

provides that “[a]ll rates and charges made, demanded, or received by any public utility for or in

connection with the transmission or sale of electric energy subject to the jurisdiction of the

Commission, . . . shall be just and reasonable, and any such rate or charge that is not just and

reasonable is hereby declared to be unlawful.” 6 In practice, Section 205 functions to confer rights

on utilities to seek rate changes while affording the Commission an opportunity to review them

solely to determine whether they are just and reasonable before the changes go into effect. 7 As the

D.C. Circuit has explained, once a utility proposes rate changes, “FERC can then review those

changes under section 205 . . . but it can reject them only if it finds that the changes proposed by

the public utility are not ‘just and reasonable.’” 8 Put differently, the Commission “must accept

proposed rate changes filed under Section 205 so long as the changes are just and reasonable.” 9

As a result, the D.C. Circuit and the Commission have both recognized that “Section 205 puts

FERC in a ‘passive and reactive role,’” responding to utility proposals and assessing whether those

proposals are just and reasonable. 10 The Commission has the binary options of either “accept[ing]

or reject[ing] the proposal,”11 with rejection generally warranted only if the Commission finds that

the proposed rate changes “are not ‘just and reasonable.’”12

7

8
  Atl. City Elec. Co., 295 F.3d at 9 (emphasis added) (citation omitted).
9
  NRG, 862 F.3d at 113 (emphasis added).
10

2007); City of Winnfield v. FERC, 744 F.2d 871, 875-76 (D.C. Cir. 1984); Midcontinent Indep. Sys.
Operator, Inc., 145 FERC ¶ 61,038, at P 6 (2013) (on rehearing).
11
   NRG, 862 F.3d at 114; see Advanced Energy Mgmt. All., 860 F.3d at 663.
12
   Atl. City Elec. Co., 295 F.3d at 9 (citation omitted).

                                                  5
         The Commission failed to adhere to these statutory requirements here. It rejected the

Notice without making the mandatory determination as to the justness and reasonableness of that

proposed change.      The words “just and reasonable” appear nowhere in the Commission’s

determination. Nor is there any plausible argument that the Commission’s decision to decline

primary jurisdiction in effect was a finding that the Notice was unjust and unreasonable.13 Rather,

the Commission made clear that it preferred that the federal court address the contract

interpretation issues first. That is not the same as a decision that ComEd’s cancellation is unjust

and unreasonable.

        Second, the Order’s decision to punt conflicts with the timing provisions set forth in

Section 205. Under Section 205, Congress carefully specified the deadlines for Commission

action. A submission under Section 205 can take effect after 60 days’ notice “[u]nless the

Commission otherwise orders[.]”14 The Commission’s options to “otherwise order” are limited; it

can reject a submission as unjust and unreasonable, 15 or it can suspend the effectiveness of a new

rate—but “not for a longer period than five months beyond the time when it would otherwise go

into effect[.]”16 And to avoid any doubt, the statute reiterates that if a Commission order has not

been “made at the expiration of such five months, the proposed change of rate . . . shall go into

effect at the end of such period[.]”17 Consistent with the statute’s purpose to “give[] a utility the

right to file rates and terms for services rendered with its assets,” 18 Section 205 therefore ensures



13
   See, e.g., Semtek Int’l Inc., 531 U.S. at 505 (“[A]n ‘adjudication upon the merits’ is the opposite of a
‘dismissal without prejudice[.]’”).
14
   16 U.S.C. § 824d(d) (emphasis added); see also, e.g., Pub. Citizen, Inc. v. FERC, 839 F.3d 1165, 1168
(D.C. Cir. 2016) (describing Section 205 filings that “become effective by operation of law”).
15
   Atl. City Elec. Co., 295 F.3d at 9 (citation omitted).
16
   16 U.S.C. § 824d(e).
17
   Id. (emphasis added).
18
   Atl. City Elec. Co., 295 F.3d at 9.

                                                    6
 that utilities have certainty that their proposals will be swiftly considered and acted on by the

Commission.

        The Order violates these provisions of Section 205. By declining to exercise primary

jurisdiction, the Commission has placed ComEd in indefinite limbo, as ComEd must wait for

another body to act before its proposed rate change can be resolved. As a practical matter, that

result flies in the face of well-settled precedent that the Commission may not “prohibit public

utilities from filing changes in the first instance,” because “the power to initiate rate changes rests

with the utility[.]”19 And regardless of how swiftly the federal court rules here, the Order identified

no limiting principle as to how long the Commission can avoid its statutory obligations under

Section 205 by enlisting the court to resolve a disputed threshold issue. The Commission’s

maneuver therefore undermines the purpose of Section 205 and unlawfully abridges utilities’ rights

under that section.

        The Commission’s rejection “without prejudice” here implicates the same issue the D.C.

Circuit found unlawful in Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC.20 There, the court concluded that

the Commission’s prior practice of “issuing a tolling order that takes no action on the application

other than buying the Commission more time” violated the “plain statutory language and context”

of the Natural Gas Act’s 30-day deadline for resolving rehearing, a provision that parallels FPA

Section 313.21 As the court explained, the Commission effectively “rewr[ote] the statute to say

that its failure to act within thirty days means nothing; it can take as much time as it wants; and

until it chooses to act, the applicant is trapped[.]”22 Rejecting a Section 205 filing without



19
   Id. at 10.
20
   Allegheny Def. Project v. FERC, 964 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2020) (en banc).
21
   Id. at 2.
22
   Id. at 15.

                                                   7
 prejudice on primary jurisdiction grounds is no different. The Commission’s Order extinguished

ComEd’s right to change its rate within the statutorily guaranteed 60-day period, leaving ComEd

in limbo until the Commission is satisfied that the court has resolved the interpretative question—

be it days, months, or years later. As in Allegheny Defense, “the Commission has no authority to

erase and replace the statutorily prescribed jurisdictional consequences of its inaction.”23

        Third, the Order further violates Section 205 by replacing Section 205’s mandatory

scheme—in which the Commission must assess whether a proposed rate change in a jurisdictional

contract is just and reasonable within a specified time—with an atextual, discretionary

determination as to primary jurisdiction. Section 205’s mandatory directive (that the Commission

decide one way or the other on a utility’s proposed rate change) is fundamentally incompatible

with the discretion-conferring primary jurisdiction doctrine (permitting the Commission to decline

to decide certain issues). And applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine here is especially

unlawful because that doctrine “applies where a claim is originally cognizable in the courts[.]”24

The claim that matters here—whether the Notice is just and reasonable—is cognizable in no court:

the Commission has exclusive jurisdiction under Section 205 to consider cancellation of the

jurisdictional contract.25 The Commission therefore cannot rely on primary jurisdiction grounds

to decline to decide whether granting such notices would be just and reasonable.

        It would be no response for the Commission to say that the Northern District of Illinois can

answer the contract interpretation question and declare what the TSA means. That does not change

24
   W. Pac. R.R. Co., 352 U.S. at 63-64; see also, e.g., Fairless Energy, LLC v. FERC, 77 F.4th 1140, 1147
(D.C. Cir. 2023) (same); Associated Elec. Coop., Inc. v. FERC, 110 F.4th 1079, 1086 (8th Cir. 2024) (“The
doctrine of primary jurisdiction applies to claims ‘properly cognizable in court that contain some issue
within the special competence of an administrative agency’” (citation omitted)).
25
   E.g., Miss. Power & Light Co. v. Mississippi ex rel. Moore, 487 U.S. 354, 371 (1988) (“FERC has
exclusive authority to determine the reasonableness of wholesale rates.”).

                                                   8
 the reality that the Northern District of Illinois cannot accept, reject, or set an effective date for a

notice of cancellation. And that difference separates this case from the scores of cases in which

the Commission typically evaluates primary jurisdiction. Those cases arise where either the

Commission or the court could grant the requested relief, and the Commission chooses to defer to

the other tribunal. Indeed, the Order itself suggested as much when it recognized that “[u]nder

Arkla the Commission determines whether to assert jurisdiction over contractual issues otherwise

litigable in state courts” by analyzing the specified three factors.26 The Commission cannot use

primary jurisdiction as a mechanism to outsource to courts questions that it would prefer not to

answer as a matter of its own discretion. To the extent the disputed contract issues are relevant to

the Commission’s determination under Section 205, the Commission itself must decide those

questions to comply with Section 205’s scheme.

        In response to all this, all the Order offered is a string cite to three prior cases where the

Commission applied the primary jurisdiction doctrine to Section 205 notices. 27 Those authorities

are unpersuasive. They are decades old and unappealed. They do not include any meaningful

analysis as to how their unusual disposition squared with the text of Section 205, nor were such

arguments even advanced by the parties to those cases. The Commission cannot circumvent its

statutory obligations by citing other orders that themselves provide no explanation for the

unorthodox maneuver the Commission employed here.

        For these reasons, the Commission should grant rehearing, find the Notice just and

reasonable, and make it effective as of July 25, 2026, as requested.

27

(2000)).

 II.    The Commission Failed to Address ComEd’s Independent Ground for Cancelling
       the TSA Based on Its Termination of Hillwood’s Retail Application.

        ComEd explained in its Notice that cancelling the TSA is just and reasonable because

 ComEd terminated the underlying Retail Application.28 The logic is simple. “Hillwood’s TSA is

 expressly premised on an active Retail Application and unambiguously conditions its effectiveness

 on an active Retail Application.”29 ComEd’s termination “was effective when sent.”30 And the

 TSA makes clear its express “purpose” is to support Hillwood “tak[ing] retail electric delivery

 services” and that all of ComEd’s obligations under the TSA are to proceed consistent with “its

 retail electric service obligations[] and applicable Retail Service Tariffs.” 31 So when the key

 premise supporting the TSA—that Hillwood’s data center project (“Project”) is active as

 evidenced by its active Retail Application—no longer exists, “the TSA serves no purpose.” 32

 Hillwood has not challenged ComEd’s Retail Application termination before the Illinois

 Commerce Commission, which has exclusive jurisdiction over the matter. 33 Nor has it sought

 relief from the Retail Application termination in its federal court complaint. These are precisely

 the circumstances under which the Commission’s regulations require cancelling a rate. 34

        Despite reciting ComEd’s arguments, 35 the Commission did not address this issue at all in

 making its determination, let alone provide a reasoned basis why it is not just and reasonable for

                                                  10
  ComEd to cancel the TSA when the underlying Retail Application had been terminated. Rather,

 the Commission’s only basis for rejecting the Notice without prejudice was that “the Parties

 disagree as to how key terms of the Transmission Security Agreement should be interpreted, and

 that the Parties currently are involved in litigation in federal district court in Illinois regarding that

 disagreement[.]”36 But that explanation solely concerned the TSA’s letter-of-credit provision, and

 the termination of Hillwood’s Retail Application is not before the federal court. The Order,

 therefore, “failed to consider an important aspect of” the Notice,37 and is arbitrary, capricious, and

 contrary to law.

           The Commission should grant rehearing and determine that the Notice is just and

 reasonable based on ComEd’s termination of Hillwood’s Retail Application.

III.      The Commission Abused Its Discretion in Declining Primary Jurisdiction Under the
          Arkla Factors.

           Even if the Commission had authority to invoke the primary jurisdiction doctrine, the

 Commission abused its discretion and failed to engage in reasoned decisionmaking by summarily

 declining to exercise primary jurisdiction over the TSA’s interpretation. The Commission also

 failed to explain why it reached the opposite conclusion from the U.S. District Court for the

 Northern District of Illinois and failed to acknowledge its departure from Commission precedent

 asserting primary jurisdiction over analogous disputes. The Commission should grant rehearing

 to correct these fatal flaws.




 36
      Order at P 26.
 37
      State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.

                                                    11
         A.       The Commission Failed to Consider an Important Aspect of the Problem:
                 The District Court Had Stayed Litigation on Primary Jurisdiction Grounds.

        To start, the Commission failed to consider that the district court had already stayed

litigation concerning the TSA because the Commission has primary jurisdiction over the dispute.38

Instead, the Commission erroneously treated that stayed litigation as if it were “currently” ongoing

or “pending” without more. 39 The federal court, however, initially “‘stayed’ the case ‘pending

resolution in FERC.’”40 The Commission did not address the federal court’s own decision and

thus “failed to consider an important aspect of the problem.”41 And because the Commission did

not address the court’s decision, it did not (and could not) explain why it disagreed with the court,

again failing a basic requirement of reasoned decisionmaking. 42

        B.       The Commission Abused Its Discretion by Arbitrarily Applying the Arkla
                 Factors and Failing to Acknowledge On-Point Commission Precedent.

        Rehearing is also required because the Commission’s analysis of the Arkla factors was

conclusory and failed to provide a reasoned basis for the Commission’s decision. In fact, all three

Arkla factors strongly favor the Commission exercising primary jurisdiction over this matter: the

dispute’s significance to the Commission’s regulatory responsibilities, especially consumer

for uniform interpretation of the TSA’s widely used, industry-leading terms.43

       1. Regulatory responsibility. Under Arkla, the Commission considers “whether the case

is important in relation to [its] regulatory responsibilities.” 44 This dispute is at the heart of the

Commission’s efforts to safeguard customers from speculative projects and its duty under the FPA

to ensure just and reasonable rates for consumers. 45 The parties’ letter-of-credit disagreement boils

down to whether families and businesses served by ComEd, and across PJM, receive $594 million

or $1 in protection from risk of development costs if the Project fails to energize. The Commission

has repeatedly recognized the significance of this issue, recently confirming that it “must act to

address the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers due to . . . speculative transmission

service requests . . . that could result in unjust and unreasonable transmission rates.” 46

       Indeed, four Commissioners highlighted the stakes of this very dispute in their

concurrences:

       Chairman Swett & Commissioner See: “[O]ur commitment to fair cost allocation,

ratepayer protection, and regulatory clarity remains unwavering. The Commission is taking

intrepid action to ensure that transmission costs triggered by large loads are allocated fairly,

transparently, and consistently.”47

         Commissioner Rosner: “There is broad bipartisan consensus around the imperative to

shield consumers from the costs of data centers. . . . Cost-recovery agreements matter because they

enable efficient and accurate planning, and ensure that project risks stay where they belong: with

the developer, not the public.”48

        Commissioner LaCerte: “[I]nfrastructure of this consequence deserves security that

reflects its actual stakes—not a token gesture that suggests ratepayers are an afterthought.” 49 “The

idea that $1 may provide appropriate security to any such agreement strikes me as an embarrassing

legal fiction[.]”50

        Yet the Order did not engage with the significance of this dispute. 51                    Instead, the

Commission merely asserted that “to the extent that the Parties’ dispute is important to the

regulatory responsibilities of the Commission, we find that consideration does not sufficiently

outweigh the other Arkla factors[.]”52 That is no explanation at all. “[C]onclusory statements will

not do; an ‘agency’s statement must be one of reasoning.’”53

        2. Special expertise. The Commission indisputably has special expertise in the TSA, as

ComEd noted in its answer.54 The parties’ dispute requires the interpretation of a Commission-

accepted rate schedule, in light of representations made to the Commission during the approval

proceeding was whether the TSA provides adequate protection to consumers from data center

development risks. 56 That is precisely the question raised here: whether a “token” security

payment of $1 satisfies Hillwood’s obligations. As Commissioner Rosner explained, Hillwood’s

reading is inconsistent with the basis on which the Commission accepted the TSA in the first

place.57 The Commission, moreover, has special expertise in security requirements for large load

interconnection writ large; it is at the forefront of developing federal policy in this arena.58

        The Order, however, did not acknowledge the Commission’s specialized knowledge or

first-hand familiarity with the TSA.59 The Order also failed to identify what aspects of “this

particular case” made the Commission’s substantial expertise immaterial to resolving the dispute. 60
